title: Every noun has a gender
title_target: Le, la, un, une — qu'est-ce que c'est ?
goal: Understand that every French noun is masculine or feminine, choose the right article, and make nouns plural without changing their sound.
bekal: tell *le / la / l' / les* from *un / une / des*
ask what something is with *qu'est-ce que c'est ?*
make nouns plural and recognize that the -s is silent
wave: Go back to **Unit 1** first: cover the French, look at the English translation, and rebuild the whole introduction dialogue from memory — out loud.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Dans la salle de classe
dialogs.intro: Budi asks his teacher about the things around him.

lines.speaker: Prof:
lines.text: C'est une gomme. Une gomme, féminin.
lines.id: It's an eraser. Une gomme, feminine.
lines.literal: it-is a(fem.) eraser. an eraser, feminine.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: And that, is it a book?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Comment on sait si c'est masculin ou féminin ?
lines.id: How do you know if it's masculine or feminine?
lines.literal: how one knows if it-is masculine or feminine?

lines.speaker: Prof:
lines.text: On ne sait pas. On apprend le mot avec l'article.
lines.id: You don't. You learn the word with its article.
lines.literal: one not knows not. one learns the word with the-article.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Toujours ? Il n'y a pas de règle ?
lines.literal: always? it not-there has not of rule?

lines.speaker: Prof:
lines.text: Il y a des tendances, mais beaucoup d'exceptions.
lines.id: There are tendencies, but lots of exceptions.
lines.literal: it there has some tendencies, but much of exceptions.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Donc j'apprends « une table », pas « table ».
lines.literal: so I-learn a table, not table.

lines.speaker: Prof:
lines.text: Exactement ! C'est le secret. Bravo, Budi.
lines.id: Exactly! That's the secret. Well done, Budi.
lines.literal: exactly! it-is the secret. bravo, Budi.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Et au pluriel, on dit « les tables » ?
lines.id: And in the plural, you say "les tables"?
lines.literal: and in-the plural, one says the tables?

lines.speaker: Prof:
lines.text: Oui. Mais attention : le « s » ne s'entend pas.
lines.id: Yes. But careful: the "s" isn't heard.
lines.literal: yes. but attention: the s not itself-hears not.

notes: **A noun's gender can't be guessed** — and the teacher is being honest. *Le soleil* (sun) is masculine, *la lune* (moon) feminine; in German it's the other way round. English gives you no help here, since English nouns have no grammatical gender at all.
**So learn every noun with its article.** Not *table* but *une table*; not *livre* but *un livre*. This habit looks trivial in Unit 3 and decides everything by Unit 15.
**Qu'est-ce que c'est ?** looks long and scary, but it is one solid chunk you learn as is: kes-kuh-SEH. It means "what is this/that?" for things. For people, the question is *qui est-ce ?*
**Ça** is an all-purpose pointing word meaning "this" or "that", whatever the gender. The full form is *cela*, but hardly anyone uses it in conversation.
**Il y a** = "there is / there are". Literally "it there has" — it makes no sense taken apart, so don't take it apart. The negative is *il n'y a pas de…*, and notice that the article shrinks to *de*.
**Beaucoup d'exceptions**, not *beaucoup des exceptions*. After a quantity word, the article always shrinks to *de* — and before a vowel, *de* becomes *d'*.

**The plural s is completely silent.** *La table* and *les tables* sound different not because of the s but because of the article: la (LAH) versus les (LAY). That's why French articles can never be dropped — they are the only audible sign of number.

grammars.title: Eight articles that hold up all of French
body: English has "the" and "a" — French has a version of each for every gender and number. The first row points to something both speakers already know ("the book"), the second introduces something new ("a book").
after: *Le* and *la* are both cut to **l'** before a vowel or silent h — so *l'ami* and *l'amie* look and sound exactly the same. The gender only shows up in other words around them.
*Des* has no English equivalent. "I have friends" = *j'ai **des** amis*. Leaving it out is the most common beginner mistake.
⚠️ French nouns almost never stand alone. If you write a sentence and there's a noun with nothing in front of it, something is almost certainly wrong.

grammars.title: Tendencies you can partly trust
body: Not rules, just odds. Useful for guessing when you really have to, not for relying on.
after: Jobs and living beings usually have two forms: *un étudiant / une étudiante*, *un chat / une chatte*. The feminine usually just adds **-e** — and that letter makes the consonant before it heard: *étudiant* (ay-tü-DYAHN) → *étudiante* (ay-tü-DYAHNT).
Names of languages and days are always masculine: *le français*, *le lundi*. Country names follow their ending: *la France*, *le Japon*, *l'Indonésie* (feminine).

grammars.title: Être, now complete
body: The last four lines held over from Unit 1. Learn them all at once — this verb appears in almost every French sentence.
after: *Elles* is used only when **everyone** being talked about is female. Add one man to the group and the whole group becomes *ils*. The same rule applies to adjectives.
Listen: *ils sont* (eel SOHN) versus *ils ont* (eel-ZOHN, from *avoir*). The only difference is one z sound, and it is the only clue. Start training your ear now.

blocks.text: Learn this table complete with the articles. Cover the first column and say them again — if you remember the word but forget its *le* or *la*, you haven't learned it yet.
Notice that meaning and gender have nothing to do with each other. Table is feminine, chair is feminine, but book and bag are masculine — and nobody can tell you why.

blocks.title: Making plurals
items: The usual rule: add an unpronounced **-s** — *un livre → des livres*.
Endings **-eau, -eu** add **-x**: *un bateau → des bateaux*, *un cheveu → des cheveux*. The x is silent too.
The ending **-al** changes to **-aux**: *un journal → des journaux*, *un animal → des animaux*. This one **can be heard** — zhoor-NAHL becomes zhoor-NOH.
Words already ending in -s, -x or -z don't change at all: *un fils → des fils*, *un prix → des prix*.
One irregular and very common one: *un œil* (eye) → *des yeux* (day ZYUH).

exercises.prompt: Fill in le, la or l'.

items: There is a table and two chairs.
I learn the word with its article.

answers: le livre — la table — l'école — l'ordinateur — la chaise — l'ami
un stylo — une fenêtre — un téléphone — une gomme — un cahier — une porte
des livres — des tables — des journaux — des bateaux — les fils — les animaux
Qu'est-ce que c'est ? — C'est un livre. — Il y a une table et deux chaises. — J'apprends le mot avec l'article. — Il n'y a pas de règle.
